lessons.title: Understanding Market Channels and Pricing
lessons.body: When you raise pigs, you need to decide where and how to sell them. The main market channels in Africa include selling live pigs at local markets, to butcheries, to restaurants, or directly to consumers. Each channel has different prices and requirements. For example, a live pig might sell for 20,000 to 30,000 Naira in Nigeria, while a butchered carcass can fetch 35,000 to 45,000 Naira. Restaurants often pay premium prices but demand consistent size and quality. You must understand your local market: visit nearby markets, talk to butchers, and ask about current prices. Prices fluctuate with feed costs, holidays, and disease outbreaks. To get the best price, sell when demand is high, such as before Christmas, Eid, or New Year. Also consider selling in bulk to traders who come to your farm; they may offer lower prices but save you transport costs. Always negotiate. A simple rule: know your cost of production per pig. If it costs you 25,000 Naira to raise a pig to 80 kg, you need to sell above that to make a profit. Keep a notebook of prices from different buyers each week. Over time, you will see patterns and can plan your sales. Don't just accept the first offer. Build relationships with several buyers so you have options. Remember, the market channel you choose affects your profit and your workload. Selling directly to consumers takes more time but gives higher returns. Selling to traders is quicker but less profitable. Choose based on your capacity and goals.

lessons.title: Direct Marketing and Value-Added Products
lessons.body: Direct marketing means selling your pigs or pork products directly to consumers, bypassing middlemen. This can increase your profit significantly. In many African communities, you can sell pork by the kilo to neighbours, local bars, or at roadside stalls. For example, a live pig sold for 30,000 Naira might yield 60 kg of pork. If you sell that pork at 800 Naira per kg, you earn 48,000 Nairaâa 60% increase. To do this, you need a slaughter slab, basic butchery skills, and a way to keep meat cool. You can also add value by making sausages, bacon, or smoked pork. Smoked pork lasts longer without refrigeration and is popular in many areas. To start, invest in a simple smoker made from a metal drum. Season the meat with salt, pepper, and local spices, then smoke for 4-6 hours. Package in clean plastic bags or paper and label with your farm name. Sell at markets, to restaurants, or through WhatsApp groups. Another value-added product is pig feed made from local ingredients like maize, soya, and cassava peels. You can sell surplus feed to other farmers. Direct marketing requires good customer service. Be reliable, keep your products clean, and offer consistent quality. Word of mouth is powerful: a satisfied customer will tell others. You can also partner with local delivery apps or bike riders to reach more customers. Remember, value-added products have a higher profit margin but also more risk of spoilage. Start small, test the market, and scale up as you learn.

lessons.title: Record Keeping and Financial Analysis
lessons.body: Keeping records is not just for big farms; it is essential for any pig business. Without records, you cannot know if you are making a profit or loss. Start with a simple notebook or a cheap exercise book. Record every expense: feed, medicine, labour, water, electricity, and transport. Also record every income: sales of pigs, pork, manure, or other products. Write the date, description, and amount. At the end of each month, add up your total expenses and total income. Subtract expenses from income to get your profit. For example, if you spent 200,000 Naira on feed, 20,000 on medicine, and 30,000 on labour, total expenses = 250,000 Naira. If you sold pigs for 350,000 Naira, your profit is 100,000 Naira. But that is not the whole story. You also need to account for the cost of piglets, depreciation of equipment, and your own time. A simple tool is a cash book, which you can buy at any stationery shop. For better analysis, use a spreadsheet on a phone or computer. Track key numbers: feed conversion ratio (kg feed per kg gain), mortality rate, and average daily gain. If your feed conversion is above 3.5, you are wasting money. If mortality is above 5%, investigate disease or management issues. Financial analysis helps you make decisions: should you buy more piglets? Change feed? Increase prices? Compare your performance month to month. Also calculate your break-even point: the number of pigs you must sell to cover all costs. For example, if each pig costs 25,000 Naira to raise and sells for 35,000, you need to sell 10 pigs to cover 250,000 Naira in fixed costs. Keep records for at least three years to see trends and plan for the future.

lessons.title: Budgeting and Cost Control
lessons.body: A budget is a plan for how you will spend and earn money. For pig farming, you need both an operating budget (monthly expenses) and a capital budget (large purchases like pens, water tanks, or a feed mixer). Start by listing all your expected costs for the next 6 months. Feed is usually 60-70% of total costs. For a farm with 20 pigs, you might need 2,000 kg of feed per month at 500 Naira per kg = 1,000,000 Naira. Add labour (maybe 50,000 Naira), veterinary services (30,000 Naira), water and electricity (20,000 Naira), and miscellaneous (20,000 Naira). Total monthly expenses = 1,120,000 Naira. Now estimate income: if you sell 10 pigs per month at 35,000 Naira each, that's 350,000 Naira. You are running at a loss! So you must either reduce costs or increase income. Cost control means finding cheaper feed ingredients, buying in bulk, or reducing waste. For example, mix your own feed using maize, soya, and fishmeal. Buy maize directly from farmers after harvest when prices are low. Store it properly to avoid aflatoxin. Control labour costs by involving family members or using part-time workers. Reduce mortality by vaccinating and keeping pens clean. Also, consider raising pigs to heavier weights to get better prices per kg. But don't overfeed; find the optimal weight. A budget helps you set targets and monitor performance. Review your budget every month. If you overspend on feed, adjust next month. Use a simple envelope system: put cash for each expense category in separate envelopes. When the envelope is empty, you cannot spend more. This teaches discipline. Remember, a budget is a tool, not a punishment. It helps you achieve your goals.

lessons.title: Risk Management and Insurance
lessons.body: Pig farming has many risks: disease outbreaks, feed price increases, theft, and natural disasters. You cannot eliminate all risks, but you can reduce their impact. The first step is to identify your risks. Common ones in Africa include African Swine Fever (ASF), which can kill all your pigs in days. Other risks: power outages affecting refrigeration, water shortages, and market price crashes. To manage disease risk, practice strict biosecurity: limit visitors, disinfect boots and vehicles, quarantine new pigs for 2 weeks, and vaccinate against common diseases like swine fever and erysipelas. Keep a footbath at the entrance. If ASF is in your area, do not buy pigs from unknown sources. For financial risk, diversify your income: sell pork, manure, and piglets. Do not rely on one buyer. Keep some cash reserve for emergencies. Insurance for pig farms is available in some African countries, but often expensive and not well developed. Check with local agricultural insurance schemes or cooperatives. In Nigeria, the Nigerian Agricultural Insurance Corporation (NAIC) offers livestock insurance. The premium might be 5-10% of the value of your pigs. For a farm with 20 pigs worth 600,000 Naira, you might pay 30,000-60,000 Naira per year. That can save you from total loss. If insurance is not available, form a savings group with other farmers. Each member contributes monthly, and the fund helps anyone who suffers a loss. Also, write a simple risk management plan: list each risk, its likelihood, and what you will do. For example, if feed prices rise, you will switch to alternative ingredients. If a disease outbreak occurs, you will cull and disinfect. Share this plan with your family and workers. Being prepared reduces panic and losses.

lessons.title: Developing a Business Plan
lessons.body: A business plan is a written document that describes your pig farm business, your goals, and how you will achieve them. It is not just for getting a loan; it helps you think clearly and make better decisions. A simple business plan for a small pig farm should be 5-10 pages. It includes: 1) Executive Summary: a one-page overview of your farm, products, and financial needs. 2) Business Description: what you do, where you are located, and what makes you unique (e.g., organic pork, free-range). 3) Market Analysis: who your customers are, what they pay, and who your competitors are. Visit local markets and talk to potential buyers. 4) Marketing Strategy: how you will reach customersâdirect sales, butcheries, restaurants, or online. Include pricing, promotion, and distribution. 5) Operational Plan: day-to-day activitiesâfeeding, cleaning, breeding, health care. Include a production schedule. 6) Management Team: who runs the farm, their skills, and roles. 7) Financial Plan: this is the most important. Include a 3-year projection of income, expenses, and profit. Start with a monthly cash flow for the first year. List all startup costs: piglets, feed, pens, water, and equipment. Estimate your break-even point. For example, if you invest 500,000 Naira in startup and each pig gives 10,000 Naira profit, you need to sell 50 pigs to break even. Also include a loan repayment plan if you borrow. 8) Risk Management: as discussed in Lesson 5. 9) Appendices: any supporting documents, like quotes for feed or letters from buyers. Write your plan in simple language. Use a notebook or computer. Review and update it every 6 months. A good business plan helps you get funding from banks, grants, or investors. It also keeps you focused on your goals. Even if you never show it to anyone, the process of writing it will improve your farm.

quiz.explanation: Break-even is when income equals total costs, so you need to sell enough to cover costs.
